tasks.instruction: Write a formal letter to your headteacher asking for permission to arrange a classroom science display. Mention the materials you will use and how you will keep the room safe.
tasks.answer:
The Headteacher
Your School
Subject: Permission to arrange a classroom science display

Sir/Madam,
We, the students of Class Six, would like to arrange a small science display in our classroom. We have made a weather chart, paper windmills and drawings of the water cycle. Sharing these projects would help us explain what we have learnt.

We propose holding the display after lessons on a day chosen by you. We will use only paper, cardboard and other safe materials. We will not bring chemicals, sharp tools or electrical equipment. Our science teacher has agreed to guide us if permission is granted. We will keep the passages clear and clean the room afterwards.

We therefore request your permission to arrange the display.
Yours obediently,
A student of Class Six

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 200 words on A Rainy Day at School.
tasks.answer:
A Rainy Day at School

Last week I experienced a rainy day at school. The morning began with dark clouds, so I packed my books in a waterproof bag. My father reminded me to take my umbrella. By the time I reached the school gate, rain was falling steadily.

Our teachers asked us to walk carefully because the steps were wet. We left our umbrellas in the place beside the entrance and went to our classroom. From the windows, we could see raindrops making circles in the puddles. The trees looked fresh and green.

We could not play outside during the break. Instead, we stayed in the classroom and played word games. One of my friends told a funny story, and another drew a picture of the rainy playground. We shared our snacks and enjoyed the quiet time together.

The rain became lighter before the final lesson ended. We waited under the school roof until our guardians arrived. Nobody was allowed to run through the flooded part of the road. I returned home safely and dried my shoes near an open window.

The day taught me that bad weather does not have to spoil our happiness. With care, preparation and good company, even a rainy school day can become a pleasant memory.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: Our class made a small weather chart. We fixed it on the classroom wall. A thermometer helps us measure temperature. Every morning, we look at the sky. We write down whether the day is sunny or cloudy. Yesterday, there was a sudden shower. We watched it through the window. Our teacher asked us to work carefully. The chart helps us understand changes in the weather. We enjoy learning new things.

tasks.answer:
To: cousin@example.com
Subject: My visit to a boat library
Dear Cousin,
Yesterday I visited a boat library near our village. It was my first visit, and I was surprised to see so many books arranged inside a boat. The librarian welcomed us and explained the borrowing rules.

I chose a story about a child who rescues an injured bird with help from an adult. I liked the colourful pictures and the simple language. My sister borrowed an atlas, so we can learn about different places together. We must return both books when the boat visits again next month.

The visit showed me that a library does not always need a large building. I hope you can join me next time. Please tell me what you are reading now.
With love,
Your cousin

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 200 words on Helping at Home.
tasks.answer:
Helping at Home

A home is a place where people care for one another. Everyone who lives there can help to make daily life easier. As a student, I cannot do every household task, but I can take responsibility for work that is safe and suitable for my age.

I begin by keeping my own things tidy. After waking up, I fold my blanket and put my school materials in order. I do not leave books, toys or shoes where someone might trip over them. These small habits save time for the whole family.

I also help to set the table and put clean clothes in the right places. Sometimes I water the plants with my younger sister. We use a small container so that we do not waste water. An adult handles hot pans, strong cleaning products and electrical repairs.

Helping at home does not mean neglecting lessons or losing all our free time. My family shares the tasks fairly, and we make a simple plan. I still have time to study, play and rest.

Household work teaches me patience, care and cooperation. It helps me understand how much effort other people make for our comfort. When everyone contributes a little, home becomes a happier place for all of us.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: A boat library visits our village once a month. It stops near the old landing place. The librarian brings interesting books for young readers. We stand in a line while we wait. Each child can borrow one book. We must return it on time. I chose a story about a lost bird. My sister chose an atlas. We carried the books home safely. Reading gives us knowledge and pleasure.

Subject: Request for a safe bicycle-parking area
Sir/Madam,
Some students of Class Six come to school by bicycle. At present, we leave our bicycles beside the entrance. They sometimes block the path, especially when many students arrive together. We are worried that someone may trip or find it difficult to pass.

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 200 words on Walking to School Safely.
tasks.answer:
Walking to School Safely

I walk to school with my elder sister on most mornings. Our school is not far from home, but part of the route follows a busy road. We leave early so that we do not have to hurry. A safe journey is more important than arriving a few minutes sooner.

We use the footpath where one is available. If the path is blocked, we stop and choose a safe way with help from an adult. We never play, push each other or look at a phone while walking near traffic.

Crossing the road requires special care. We use the footbridge or a marked crossing whenever possible. Before stepping onto the road, we stop, look carefully in both directions and listen. We do not assume that every driver has seen us.

Rainy weather makes the journey more difficult. The ground can be slippery, and umbrellas may hide part of the road. On such days, we walk slowly and allow extra time. If the route is flooded or unsafe, our family arranges another way to reach school.

Following safety rules is a daily responsibility. I remind my friends gently when they forget. Walking carefully helps us reach school ready to learn and return home safely to the people who care for us.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: Our school held a road-safety lesson. A visitor spoke to us about crossing roads. We should stop at the kerb and look both ways. We must never run across a busy road. A footbridge is a safe place to cross. The visitor showed us a picture of a helmet. It protects our head while cycling. We should ride carefully and obey signals. We thanked the visitor for the lesson. Safety is important for everyone.

tasks.answer:
Dear Friend,
I hope you are well. Last week our class visited a local museum with two teachers. I want to tell you about the trip because I think you would enjoy the place too.

The first object that interested me was an old clay pot. The guide explained how people used similar pots to store water. I also saw a wooden model of a fishing boat. Its shape helped me understand how boats carry people and goods on our rivers.

We read the labels, asked questions and made short notes. We were careful not to touch the objects. The visit taught me that ordinary things can tell important stories about the past.

Please write about an interesting place you have visited. I would love to read your news.
Your loving friend

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 200 words on A Visit to a Local Museum.
tasks.answer:
A Visit to a Local Museum

A museum helps us learn about the past through objects, pictures and stories. Recently our class visited a local museum. Two teachers went with us, and a guide welcomed us at the entrance. Before entering, we listened to the rules and put our bags in the proper place.

The first room contained clay pots, baskets and farming tools. I had seen similar baskets in my grandmother’s house, but I had never thought of them as objects worth studying. The guide explained how their materials and shapes suited different kinds of work.

In another room, we saw model boats and photographs of river journeys. The pictures showed people carrying goods, catching fish and travelling to markets. They helped me understand the importance of rivers in everyday life.

We read the labels and asked questions politely. I made a sketch of a clay pot and wrote down two facts about it. We did not touch any display because even a small careless action could damage an old object.

After returning to school, we discussed our favourite exhibits. The visit made our history lessons feel more real. It also taught us to respect the work and skills of earlier generations. I would like to visit the museum again with my family.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: Our class visited a local museum. We arrived at ten in the morning. A guide welcomed us at the door. She showed us an old clay pot. It was kept inside a glass case. We read the labels quietly. We did not touch or move any object. The guide answered our questions. I drew a picture of the pot. The visit taught us about life in the past.

tasks.instruction: Write a formal letter to your headteacher requesting permission to establish a small seed bank. Explain its educational value and how it would be maintained.
tasks.answer:
The Headteacher
Your School
Subject: Permission to establish a small seed bank
Sir/Madam,
We, the students of Class Seven, request permission to establish a small seed bank in our school. We would like to collect seeds from common garden plants and learn how to store, label and grow them responsibly.

The project would support our science lessons. Students could compare germination and record plant growth without collecting rare or protected plants. We would use a dry cupboard selected by the science teacher and store only seeds approved as safe for classroom use. No student would taste any seed or bring pesticides to school.

A small team could check the packets weekly, keep a borrowing register and clean the storage area. We propose beginning with a few labelled packets rather than a large collection.

We therefore request your permission and a teacher’s guidance for this project.
Yours obediently,
On behalf of Class Seven

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 250 words on Learning through a School Garden.
tasks.answer:
Learning through a School Garden

A school garden can be more than a pleasant green corner. It can become an outdoor classroom where students learn by observing, asking questions and doing useful work together. Even a few pots can offer valuable lessons if they are cared for regularly.

In a garden, science becomes easier to understand. Students can watch seeds germinate, compare leaves and measure the growth of stems. They discover that plants need suitable amounts of water, light and space. Keeping records helps them notice changes that might otherwise escape attention.

Gardening also develops responsibility. A plant cannot explain that it has been forgotten, so students must follow a sensible care plan. Duties should be shared fairly, especially during holidays. Choosing common local plants and reusing safe containers can keep the project affordable.

The garden provides opportunities to practise other subjects. Students can calculate the amount of soil required for a bed, draw labelled diagrams or write descriptions of insects they observe. Group discussions encourage them to explain their ideas and listen to different suggestions.

Safety and respect for living things are important. Students should use suitable tools under adult supervision, wash their hands afterwards and avoid handling unknown plants or chemicals. They should observe small animals without harming them.

A successful school garden does not depend on producing the largest vegetables. Its real value lies in the habits it builds: patience, careful observation, teamwork and care for shared surroundings. When students see a plant grow through their own steady effort, learning becomes both memorable and rewarding.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: A group of students created a seed bank in their school. They collected seeds from local gardeners. Each packet carried a label with the plant’s name. The packets were stored in a cool, dry cupboard. Students borrowed seeds and grew them in small pots. They recorded how tall the seedlings became each week. Some plants needed more light than others. The students shared their notes and discussed the differences. Their teacher praised their patience. The project helped everyone learn about plants.

tasks.instruction: Write an informal email to your friend describing a book-repair activity at school. Explain what you did and what you learnt about caring for books.
tasks.answer:
To: friend@example.com
Subject: Our book-repair activity
Dear Friend,
Last Thursday I took part in a book-repair activity in our school library. Our librarian first explained how to handle damaged books without making the damage worse. We worked in small groups under her supervision.

My group checked for folded corners and loose covers. We placed the books on clean tables and recorded the damage. The librarian showed us which materials were suitable for simple repairs. She completed the difficult work herself. We did not use sharp tools or cover any printed words with tape.

By the end of the afternoon, several books were ready to return to the shelves. I learnt that caring for a book begins long before it becomes damaged. Clean hands, careful storage and timely returns can make a great difference.

Does your school arrange a similar activity? Please write and share your experience.
Your friend

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 250 words on Caring for Shared Property.
tasks.answer:
Caring for Shared Property

Shared property includes the desks, library books, playground equipment and other facilities that many people use together. These things may not belong to one student personally, but that does not make them less valuable. Caring for them is a practical way to show respect for others.

At school, small careless actions can create lasting problems. Writing on a desk spoils the working space of the next class. Tearing a library page prevents another reader from understanding a story. Leaving a tap running wastes water that the whole community needs.

Good habits begin with ordinary choices. We should use equipment for its intended purpose, return borrowed materials and keep shared spaces tidy. If something is broken, we should tell a responsible adult instead of hiding the damage or attempting a dangerous repair ourselves.

Schools can support these habits by providing clear instructions and listening to students. Sometimes damage occurs because a shelf is overcrowded or a door is difficult to close. Reporting such problems helps adults make sensible improvements. Students should be encouraged to speak honestly without fear of unfair blame.

Caring for shared property also teaches us about fairness. Everyone deserves a clean classroom and safe facilities, including those who will join the school after us. Money spent replacing avoidably damaged objects cannot be used for new books or activities.

Responsibility does not end at the school gate. The same care should guide us in parks, buses and public libraries. When we protect common resources, we help create places that are welcoming and useful for everyone.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: Our school started a repair corner for damaged books. A teacher showed us how to work carefully. We placed each book on a clean table. Torn pages were joined with suitable tape. We did not cover any printed words. A loose cover needed more care than a folded corner. We asked an adult for help with difficult repairs. Each repaired book received a small record card. The activity taught us to value books and reduce waste. We felt proud of our work.

tasks.instruction: Write a formal email to a local craftsperson inviting them to speak at a school craft session. Explain the purpose, audience and proposed arrangements.
tasks.answer:
To: guest@example.com
Subject: Invitation to a school craft session
Sir/Madam,
We are writing on behalf of our Class Seven activity group to invite you to speak at a school craft session. We would like our classmates to learn how local crafts are made and why these skills remain valuable.

The session would take place in a classroom with a teacher present. You could explain the main stages of your work and show a few safe, finished examples. We do not expect you to bring heavy equipment or carry out any hazardous process. Students would prepare questions and listen respectfully.

Our teacher will contact you to agree on a convenient date and discuss travel or material costs before confirming the event. We will not announce your participation without your agreement.

We hope you will consider our invitation. Please let us know whether you are interested and what arrangements would be suitable.
Yours faithfully,
The Class Seven activity group

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 250 words on Learning from Local Craftspeople.
tasks.answer:
Learning from Local Craftspeople

Local craftspeople turn knowledge, practice and simple materials into useful or beautiful objects. Potters, weavers, basket makers and other skilled workers often learn through years of observation and effort. Students can gain a deeper understanding of their community by learning about this work respectfully.

A conversation with a craftsperson can connect classroom lessons with everyday life. A potter may explain how the condition of clay affects a bowl. A weaver may demonstrate a repeating pattern. Such examples help students see science, mathematics and design working together.

Learning from a craftsperson should not mean treating the person as a free source of entertainment. A school must agree on the purpose, time and costs of a visit in advance. The guest’s permission is also needed before photographs or recordings are shared. Respect includes recognising that skilled work supports a person’s livelihood.

Students have responsibilities too. They should prepare thoughtful questions, listen without interrupting and handle any displayed objects only when invited. Hazardous processes and tools should remain in trained adult hands. A safe demonstration can be interesting without allowing everyone to operate equipment.

Afterwards, students can discuss what surprised them and compare different stages of the work. They might draw a process diagram or write a short report. They should credit the person who shared the knowledge rather than presenting it as their own discovery.

Local crafts are not simply reminders of the past. They can develop and adapt to new needs. Meeting the people behind them encourages curiosity, appreciation and respect for patient, skilled human effort.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: A school radio team prepared a short programme about local crafts. They invited a potter to speak about her work. Before the interview, the students wrote clear questions. They tested the microphone before the recording began. The potter explained that clay must be prepared carefully. She showed them an unfinished bowl. The students listened with interest and did not interrupt. Afterwards, they thanked their guest. The programme helped others learn about a useful craft. It also made the team more confident.

tasks.instruction: Write an informal letter to your cousin describing a school water-saving survey. Explain the problem you found, how it was reported and what changed afterwards.
tasks.answer:
Dear Cousin,
I hope you are keeping well. Our class recently carried out a water-saving survey at school. I had never noticed how much water could be wasted by a tap that did not close properly.

We worked in pairs and recorded the condition of the taps. My partner and I found a steady leak near the playground. We wrote down its location and informed our teacher. We did not try to repair it ourselves because we lacked the tools and training.

The caretaker arranged for a worker to replace a damaged washer. We checked the tap afterwards and were pleased to see that it closed properly. Our group also made a poster reminding everyone to report leaks promptly.

The activity taught me that noticing a problem is only the first step. Reporting it clearly and following up can lead to a useful change. Please tell me about a practical project at your school.
With love,
Your cousin

tasks.instruction: Write a composition of about 250 words on Using Water Responsibly at School.
tasks.answer:
Using Water Responsibly at School

Clean water is needed for drinking, washing and keeping school facilities usable. Although students may see water flowing from a tap every day, the supply should not be taken for granted. Responsible use means meeting real needs without unnecessary waste. It does not mean avoiding proper handwashing or drinking too little.

A school can begin by looking for simple problems. A tap that keeps dripping or a damaged pipe may waste water for hours. Students can report the location of a leak to a teacher or caretaker. Repairs should be carried out by trained adults, not by children experimenting with unfamiliar tools.

Daily habits matter as well. We should turn taps off properly after use and use only the water we need. When cleaning classrooms, staff can choose sensible methods rather than leaving a hose running without purpose. Clear signs can remind users, but signs alone cannot fix faulty equipment.

Students can take part in safe awareness activities. A small survey might record which taps need attention, while a poster could explain how to report a problem. Any measurement activity must avoid wasting water simply to demonstrate that waste exists.

Schools also need reliable maintenance and access to safe drinking water. Responsibility should not be placed entirely on individual children when broken facilities make good habits difficult. Adults must respond to reports and keep students informed about improvements.

Using water carefully connects personal behaviour with shared management. When students and staff work together, they can protect a useful resource while keeping health, comfort and cleanliness at the centre of school life.

editorialChecks.completedCloze: Our class organised a survey about the school water taps. We worked in pairs and checked each tap. We did not attempt any repairs ourselves. Instead, we wrote down where water was leaking. One tap was harder to close than the others. We reported it to the caretaker. A worker replaced a damaged washer. The tap then closed properly. We made posters to remind everyone to turn taps off after use. The survey helped us notice a problem we had ignored. Saving water is our shared responsibility.
